l: forms, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Forms signify things, Gods, or wild beasts, and are changed by the Gods into new bodies in The Metamorphoses.

l: new bodies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The new bodies result from forms being changed.

l: the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Gods are deities of Heaven who inhabit the court of heaven, possess its tract in animated forms, and can change forms into new bodies. The speaker opens by asking their favor. They assemble in Jupiter’s marble hall to hear accusations against the human race and Lycaon, assent to vengeance, and become silent at Jupiter’s command. Their power is central: they are invoked for relief, worshipped and prayed to, restore Pelops, change Narcissus into a flower, transform Nyctimene into an owl and Ocyrrhoe into a mare, and make the immortal Chiron mortal. They are also linked to limits on restoring life against their will, permit Pyramus and Thisbe’s deaths and burial, and are appealed to in Cadmus’s and Hermione’s transformations. They have made Cadmus’s daughter and grandson sea deities. Finally, they vanquish Typhœus and throw Ætna upon his body.

l: narrative, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Metamorphoses is a lengthened narrative extending from the world's beginning to the speaker's own times.

l: universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The universe, or world, begins as Chaos: sea, earth, and heaven mixed together. From separated pre-existent matter, its architect arranges the elements into an ordered creation of land, waters, air, heavens, climates, stars, and living creatures. It provides the narrative’s starting point. Because the impious human race commits grave crimes, Jupiter threatens the world with ruin and floods it, leaving only Deucalion and Pyrrha alive. After Jupiter disperses clouds and the waters recede, the world is restored, though it seems empty and silent to Deucalion.

l: times (the speaker's own), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The speaker’s own times provide the ending point for the lengthened narrative.

l: Augustus Cæsar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Augustus Cæsar is a Roman ruler residing in Palatium, whose days define the author’s own times. An impious band sought to extinguish the Roman name in his blood, alarming humanity and shaking the earth with horror.

l: Nature, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bounteous Nature, an invisible agency of the Deity, joins God to end Chaos, orders the elements, makes water common, and leaves Cadmus a hissing voice.

l: Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ocean is an unnavigable sea and expanse of water that, after separating from earth, heaven, and air, sinks to the lowest place and surrounds Earth. It expands in the deluge, overwhelms hills and mountain heights, loses distinct shores, and carries away people, animals, buildings, and vegetation. Neptune raises or calms it and orders its retreat, after which it again has a shore. Jupiter later crosses it as a bull carrying Europa, who fears the passage and looks back toward shore.

l: Earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Earth begins without firmness, mixed with sea and air, then is separated from heaven and waters, settles beneath lighter elements, draws ponderous atoms, and is pressed together by its own gravity. In its ordered shape it is a vast, even globe: sea surrounds its shores, and it contains rivers, lakes, woods, mountains, five climates, and five zones corresponding to those in the heavens. It is at first free from harrow and ploughshare, producing grain and other sustenance of its own accord; later Ceres’s seeds are buried in furrows, land is divided by boundaries, and its entrails are mined for riches. It also provides material for Prometheus to fashion Man. Earth suffers from human wickedness, slaughter, and the blood of the Giants’ sons. From that warm gore it gives life and shapes a generation of men as a memorial of the ruthless race. Jupiter surveys it in human shape and determines its punishment by deluge. Neptune opens its waters with his trident; sea covers its plains, hills, groves, fields, houses, and temples, leaving desolate silence. When waters subside, hills, ground, places, and woods reappear. As the great mother, Earth’s stones are understood as its bones. A fertile source of living forms, Earth produces animals when moisture, heat, and sun-warmed soil are properly mixed. After the deluge it restores former shapes and creates new monsters, including Python. It delivers oracles at Delphi before Themis, is invoked by Daphne, and is called a genial, all-productive goddess. Its bowels hide springs; it produces leaves, corn, and frankincense, receives tears, trembles under Typhœus, and requests Jupiter to end destructive fire. It is covered by darkness during Jupiter’s pursuit of Io, and later is scorched by Phaëton’s chariot, begging the ruler of the gods to save the universe.

l: Heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Heaven is a lofty, weightless fiery realm of æther in the highest region, covering the universe and resting on Atlas's mountain form with many stars. At first it covers all things, mixed with earth, sea, and air; once distinguished from gross atmosphere, it rises highest. Giants seek sovereignty by stacking Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa, while Calisto and Arcas become neighboring constellations.

l: Air, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Air begins mixed with land and sea and void of light; once separated, it stands next to heaven, heavier than fire and lighter than water, contains clouds, transmits light, and belongs by nature to no one.

l: four elements, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_combined harmonious unison [each in its proper place] The elements are initially confused and discordant, with cold opposed to hot, moist to dry, soft to hard, and heavy things to weightless things. God and bounteous Nature separate them and place them in harmonious order.

l: world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The world’s formation is preserved in a confused mythological tradition about ordering Chaos, with a faint reflection of the creation account in the Book of Genesis. It begins in the Golden Age, governed by Innocence and Justice without threats or soldiers. After Saturn’s expulsion it falls under Jupiter and declines through changing ages into Iron Age violence and corruption. Ceres’s search damages its fertility.

l: Apollo, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Apollo is presented chiefly as a god: an ennobled deity, supposed son of Hyperion and also called a son of Jupiter, Pythian God, God of Delphi, Delian God, Phœbus, and the Sun. He is an ever-youthful archer, healer, oracle, musician, and world-governing power, born on Delos and associated with the Sun, healing herbs, prophecy, victory, arrows, the harp, bow, lyre, and plectrum. His worship at Delphi is said not yet to have been known in Deucalion’s time; one explanation alternatively presents him as a god, prince, or priest who destroyed Python or a robber. After subduing Python, Apollo proudly mocks Cupid, but Cupid makes him love Daphne. He pursues and praises her; when she becomes a laurel, he claims the tree for his hair, lyre, and quiver and grants it lasting honor. He gives oracles at Patara for six months yearly and is linked with healing, though herbs cannot cure his love. As Phaëton’s claimed father, he is the Sun governing the world. After Phaëton’s death, he appears eclipsed and grief-stricken, withholds services from the world, and challenges Jupiter or another God to drive the chariot of light. He also loves Coronis: after hearing the raven’s report, he kills her, regrets it, rescues their child from the flames, and punishes the raven by barring it from white birds. Later, while in Elis and the Messenian fields, he tends cattle in shepherd’s clothing, occupied with love and pipe music, and Mercury steals stray cattle. Apollo is associated with plague and is said to have killed Niobe’s sons with arrows. Finally, challenged by Marsyas in music, he wins, fastens Marsyas to a tree, flays him, suspends his skin in Celenæ, and delivers his body to Olympus for burial.

l: Neptune, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Neptune is an ennobled deity, god and ruler of the deep, waters, and sea, retaining sovereignty after deification and receiving the empire of the sea in the world's division. A king perhaps originally of a separate kingdom, he commands the waters with his three-forked trident: during the deluge he assists Jupiter, summons rivers to pour out their force, and opens Earth’s water sources; afterward he calms the waves and orders Triton to call sea and rivers back within their bounds. He raises as well as calms the sea. He compassionately transforms Ino and Melicerta, removing their mortality and making them the sea deities Leucothoë and Palæmon. At the Nereids’ request he sends a sea monster against the Ethiopians, and he presents a bull to Minos. In the dispute with Minerva over Athens, he is overcome; the account associates him with navigation, piracy, the sea, and the horse.

l: God as architect of the universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: In an ancient philosophical system, God, distinguished from creator, acts as Architect, arranging and disposing pre-existent elements into places suited to their respective qualities.

l: the creation of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The creation of the world, explained by Moses in the first chapters of Genesis and contrasted with mythological accounts of Chaos, unfolds by separating and ordering matter, forming land, waters, climates, winds, stars, and creatures, then forming man last to rule the rest.

l: Hesiod, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Hesiod is a heathen writer, identified as the most ancient to enlarge on the world's formation. He is first among the poets discussed to mention Chaos, draws much formation material from Sanchoniatho, and records the tradition of Phaëton and his sisters.

l: Genesis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Genesis is a book of Holy Writ and Scripture. Its opening two chapters recount the world's formation: darkness lies over the deep, light is created, and man appears as the Creator's last work, receiving dominion over fish, birds, and other living things. It unfolds from darkness and creation to humanity's appointed rule.

l: Scriptures, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: relate histories of Adam and Noah [as events that really happened] The Scriptures relate the corresponding events in the histories of Adam and Noah.

l: Sanchoniatho, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Sanchoniatho is a heathen writer said to have lived before the Trojan War and written originally in Phoenician. He claimed Jerombaal as his source on the world’s original construction; his works survive in translation through Philo Judaeus and are considered spurious by many.

l: Greeks, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Greeks borrowed notions about Chaos, probably from Sanchoniatho, and often embellished their mythology with narratives of Phoenician or Egyptian origin. After Cadmus’s death, they reported that he and Hermione became serpents, perhaps referring to his Phoenician origin. They were initiated into the mysteries of Ceres, with Celeus, Triptolemus, Eumolpus, and Diocles among the first. In later ages they arrived in Sicily, where they associated their river Alpheus with the Fountain of Arethusa because of similar names, and they received the golden fleece as treasure brought into Grecian cities.

l: Prometheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Prometheus is a figure in heathen Mythology and son of Iapetus. He tempers earth with water and fashions Man in the image of the Gods, then is associated with teaching mankind to make fire and with metalworking. He is father of Deucalion and is identified by some writers with Noah or Magog.

l: Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Minerva is a goddess, divine female warrior, daughter of Jupiter, and a warlike, yellow-haired virgin also called Tritonia and Pallas. She springs from Jupiter’s head and is said to have been born near Trito. She animates Man and Prometheus’s workmanship, and with Prometheus represents formation and animation of man. She is patroness and tutelary divinity of Athens, associated with and owning the olive tree, and is credited by some with making linen cloths and nets. Her actions emphasize guarded divine secrets, counsel, rivalry, and punishment. She hides Ericthonius in a basket, entrusts it to three virgins, forbids inquiry, and withdraws protection from a virgin after Aglauros’s disobedience is reported. Angered that Aglauros revealed her mysteries, she commands the hated Envy to make Aglauros jealous of Herse. As Cadmus’s favorer, she directs him to sow dragon’s teeth, producing armed earth-born warriors. She punishes impiety, changes Medusa’s hair to serpents, gives Perseus a reflecting shield, and accompanies him until leaving Seriphus. After traveling to Mount Helicon and visiting the Muses, she becomes Arachne’s rival. Disguised as an old woman, she warns Arachne, reveals herself, weaves a web of Athens and divine contests, then tears Arachne’s excellent web, strikes her, and transforms her into a spider. She also plays the flute but throws it aside in disgust after seeing its effect on her appearance.

l: rivers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Rivers, obeying Neptune, open their fountains, flow unobstructed to the sea, cross plains, and sweep away crops, groves, flocks, people, houses, temples, and sacred utensils.

l: the water, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Water, heavier than air and common to all yet owned by no one, is denied and muddied by countrymen as Latona seeks relief, prompting her curse.

l: Persia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Persia, also called Achæmenian after a former king, is a region celebrated by poets for frankincense and other aromatic plants, possibly introduced by Orchamus.

l: Scythia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Scythia, an extreme northern kingdom ruled by Lyncus, receives Triptolemus during his journey.

l: mankind, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Mankind is an animated human race, the Creator’s last work, formed from earth tempered with water and made in the image of the Gods. More fitted for higher faculties than other creatures, it has an upright countenance turned toward heavens and stars and rules over animals, fish, and birds. It begins with primeval innocence but gradually degenerates into a greatly wicked, universally corrupt, impious race, whose thoughts are continually evil. Condemned by Jupiter and marked to be cut off wherever Nereus roars, it is threatened with destruction so corruption will not spread. Its loss is repaired by Deucalion and Pyrrha: stones become a renewed generation, hardy and able to endure fatigue.

l: mortals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Mortals, or mankind, begin in the Golden Age living safely and peacefully, without avengers, war, or shores beyond their own, sustained by freely produced natural food. They become universally corrupt and wicked, so Jupiter condemns them to deserved vengeance. A universal deluge destroys the human race beneath the waves; most perish or later succumb to hunger. In the end, only Deucalion and Pyrrha remain, and Deucalion longs to restore the lost people by molding earth and giving it souls.

l: Alpheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Alpheus is a river, also described as a stream of Elis, rising in Arcadia, running through the Eleans’ territory, disappearing underground and reappearing, and entering the sea near Cyllene. In the poetic story, he sees Arethusa bathing, loves and relentlessly pursues her across regions; after she becomes a stream, he changes from mortal form into water to mingle with her.

l: the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun is a God, son of Hyperion, eye of the universe, author of light, and ruler of all things by radiant æthereal light. It possesses light, heat, horses, a disk, and the chariot driven by Phaëton; it moves in the ecliptic, measures the long year, and dissipates noxious exhalations after the receding waters. It is associated with Scripture and traditions of standing still upon Gibeon or of a backward-moving shadow. After Phaëton’s death, the Sun hides its sorrow-darkened face, suffers an eclipse of its disk, and refuses to drive the light-bearing chariot; one day passes without the sun. First to discover Venus and Mars’s adultery, it tells Vulcan. Venus’s retaliation causes excessive love for Leucothoë: the Sun neglects its course, disguises itself as Eurynome, embraces her, mourns her burial, and changes her into a frankincense tree. It ends intercourse with and despises Clytie, who continues longing for it.

l: Italy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_the_scene_of Golden Age [according to Latin writers] Italy was identified by the Latin writers as the setting for the events associated with the Golden Age.

l: flames, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Flames, produced from flint and steel, spread from the chariot through heaven, earth, and sea, burning clouds, lands, peoples, waters, and Phaëton’s yellow hair. They threaten the universe and world’s destruction until Jupiter restrains them with ruthless fires; afterward they provide light when the Sun’s face is hidden.

l: Noah, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Noah is a just man included in histories related by Scriptures, identified by some writers with Prometheus and compared with Deucalion. Saved with his family for virtuous conduct, he leaves the ark and offers solemn sacrifices to God.

l: four ages of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: follow formation of man [in succession] The four ages of the world follow the formation of man. The Golden Age is the first of them.

l: Golden Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Golden Age is the first of the four ages, a period of greater happiness associated with the more happy days of the first parents. Founded first and governed by Innocence and Justice, it is marked by people practising faith and rectitude without laws, punishment, war, or fear, while Earth provides abundant food. Perpetual spring prevails and seasons are unknown. Its people are more just and happier than those of the Silver Age. Yet the account is inconsistent: wars and crimes are also said to occur during it.

l: Innocence, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: governed world [during the Golden Age] Innocence governs the world during the Golden Age.

l: Justice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: governed world [during the Golden Age] Justice governs the world during the Golden Age.

l: laws, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Laws are publicly inscribed rules absent in the Golden Age, when men practise faith and rectitude without governance.

l: mountains, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: facilitate assault on heaven [by being heaped together] The Giants heap mountains together in an assault on heaven, piling them up to the lofty stars. The mountains then overwhelm and bury the Giants.

l: perpetual spring, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: existed present [during the Golden Age] An eternal spring exists during the Golden Age. Gentle Zephyrs foster flowers that grow without seed.

l: heathen poets, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Heathen poets probably learned traditions of the first parents’ peaceful innocence, Eden’s abundance, and the fall’s effects; they recast this happier time as a Golden Age in their own countries, disfiguring the original story through fanciful marvels.

l: tradition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Tradition preserves memories of the first parents’ peaceful innocence, a divine decision to punish the earth by a deluge, and one just man surviving universal corruption. Transmitted to heathen poets and preserved by Greeks, Romans, and all nations, it unfolds in Ovid’s Deucalion account, where sea waters join those from heaven; Deucalion corresponds to Noah in Scripture.

l: first parents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: live_in peaceful innocence [for some time] The first parents initially lived in peaceful innocence. They had abundant food without tillage, and the animals were submissive to their commands.

l: garden of Eden, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: furnish fruit and food [in abundance and without tillage] The garden of Eden furnished the first parents with fruit and food in abundance without tillage.

l: fall, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Fall causes the ground’s unfruitfulness, requiring labor, and ends nature’s spontaneous acknowledgment of man as master.

l: Latin writers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: place Golden Age [in Italy under the reigns of Saturn and Janus] The Latin writers placed in Italy, under the reign of Saturn and Janus, events that the Scriptures relate in the histories of Adam and Noah.

l: Saturn, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Saturn, father of Uranus, expels his father and seizes the throne. He reigns over Italy’s Golden Age, linked to perpetual spring but also wars and crimes. Before Jupiter rules the world, Saturn is driven into Tartarus.

l: Janus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: reigns_over Italy [in the Latin writers' account of the Golden Age] Janus was described as reigning with Saturn over the events that Latin writers placed in Italy and associated with the Golden Age.

l: Silver Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Silver Age is the second age, succeeding the Golden Age under Jupiter's rule. Less just and happy than the Golden Age, yet more valuable than the Brazen Age, it divides the year into four seasons as men build primitive houses, bury seeds, and plow with oxen.

l: Brazen Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Brazen Age, the third age after Silver Age, begins with fiercer people prone to horrible warfare yet free from impiety.

l: Iron Age, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Iron Age is the last age, succeeding the Brazen Age and still continuing. It marks humanity’s degeneration into wickedness and impiety, with vice and every species of crime: fraud, deceit, treachery, violence, greed, warfare, murder, and collapsed family loyalty.

l: humanity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: derive_origin_from blood [the generation is formed from the Giants' blood] Humanity becomes progressively less virtuous after the Golden Age. Men begin making shelters, farming, sailing, measuring and claiming land, mining for riches, and committing violence, betrayal, murder, and other crimes.

l: agriculture, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Agriculture is treated through Ceres, whose buried seeds, teaching of tilling and sowing corn, and returning crops support her interpretation as goddess of the Earth and corn. Though linked to its introduction into Greece, the account favors the introduction of Ceres's worship, while allowing improved tilling methods from Egypt.

l: War, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: War emerges with destructive iron and gold, using violence and brandishing clattering weapons in blood-stained hands.

l: crime, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: bursts_forth_in Iron Age [every species] Crime bursts forth in the Iron Age in every form. It includes fraud, deceit, treachery, violence, greed, rapine, murder, and the poisoning of family members.

l: wickedness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Vice is encouraged by the riches dug from the Earth, which had hidden them and removed them to the Stygian shades. Its rise accompanies the degeneration of the Iron Age.

l: Astræa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Astræa is a virgin heavenly deity and Goddess of Justice, variously said to be daughter of Astræus and Aurora or of Jupiter and Themis. Last of the heavenly deities to abandon Earth, she leaves only when it is drenched in slaughter, then takes her place among the stars as the Constellation of the Virgin.

l: aconite, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Aconite, or wolfsbane, was said to grow abundantly near Acherusia after Cerberus was dragged through the cavern; named from the Greek for whetstone, it is poisonous and mixed in pretended enchantments.

l: Infernal Regions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Infernal Regions are Pluto’s low-lying western kingdom, imagined as eternally dark and associated with subterranean mines. Their threshold is Avernus, and they contain the burning river Phlegethon and Tityus’s punishment. Proserpine is carried there to become queen and spouse of the Infernal King; Jupiter makes her return depend on whether she has eaten there, and she must ultimately spend part of each year with Pluto. They are proposed to derive from Egyptian notions of the future state of man.

l: gold, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a sinew of war [perhaps more properly than iron] Aglauros demands gold of great weight as payment for helping Mercury gain access to Herse. Minerva reflects that Aglauros might be enriched by taking the gold she has demanded.

l: Themis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Themis is a sacred prophetic Goddess, daughter of Cœlus and Terra, whose Greek name means what is just and right. She gives sacred oracular responses, precedes Apollo at Delphi, has a temple and an ancient oracle in Bœotia, and instructs men to ask the Gods what is lawful. After Deucalion and Pyrrha reach Parnassus, they consult her neglected temple; moved by prayer, she gives the response renewing humanity.

l: attempt by the giants to reach heaven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Giants attempt to reach heaven by piling mountains atop one another, an act possibly based on building the tower of Babel.

l: blood, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Warm, plenteous gore of Giants’ sons drenches Earth, gives life to a generation whose violence and greed reflect its bloody origin.

l: generation sprung from the blood of the Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A generation of men, formed by Earth from the warm blood of the Giants’ sons, despises the Gods above and is defined by ruthless slaughter and violence.

l: Thessaly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Thessaly is a chalky, mountainous region containing Peneus, near horsemen and associated with magicians. During Deucalion’s reign, stopped Peneus and extraordinary rain flooded it; it was generally identified with the deluge, though one narrative made the flood universal.

l: the war of the Gods with the Giants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_distinct_from war between Jupiter and the Titans The war of the giants is distinguished from the war between Jupiter and the Titans. It concerns the Giants’ attempt to reach heaven.

l: Titans, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Titans are inhabitants of heaven, described in notes as possibly arising from traditions about the fall of the angels.

l: fall of the angels, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A tradition, possibly giving rise to the story of the Titans, is conveyed as the fall of the angels.

l: angels, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The angels are said to have fallen, according to tradition, and this fall may have contributed to the story of the Titans.

l: tower of Babel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The tower of Babel is a building whose construction may have inspired giants' attempted ascent to heaven.

l: Cain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cain is a first murderer, possibly original to Lycaon; he murders Abel during sacrifice, is called to account by Almighty, and is sentenced to be a fugitive and wanderer on earth.

l: descendants of Cain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Descendants of Cain are probably identified with Scripture’s children “of men” and giants, and may be depicted as Giants and a generation sprung from their blood.

l: Scripture, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: relates deluge [the determination of the Almighty to punish the earth] Scripture records that God saw mankind's great wickedness and determined to destroy man, beast, creeping thing, and the fowls of the air from the earth.

l: grand council of the Gods, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The grand council of the Gods, summoned by Jupiter, meets without delay in the heavenly assembly hall to deliberate how to punish mankind for the crimes of its impious, wicked race.

l: Lycaon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Lycaon is an Arcadian king and tyrant associated with a polluted banquet, remarkable cruelty, impiety, and a plot against Jupiter. When Jupiter comes as a guest, Lycaon mocks the people’s prayers and tests whether Jupiter is a God or mortal by planning to kill him. He cuts the throat of a Molossian hostage, cooks the body, and serves human flesh at a feast. Jupiter punishes him by destroying his house and transforming him into a wolf. The records also preserve conflicting reports: Pausanias and Suidas call him a virtuous prince, benefactor, and promoter of improvement, and the story is possibly based on Cain.

l: Hercules, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Hercules, the Tirynthian hero, is suckled by Juno and named as Zeus/Jupiter’s son. He slays Hydra, takes Cos’s chief city, drags and chains Cerberus from Tartarus, and dies on a ridge of Œta.

l: Vulcan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Vulcan is an ennobled deity, described as Juno’s son or the only son of Jupiter and Juno, and Venus’s husband. Precipitated from heaven for deformity, he falls on Lemnos, where he works as a blacksmith and divine craftsman, creating Phaëton’s chariot. Told by the Sun of Venus’s affair with Mars, he fashions nearly invisible brass chains and nets, traps the lovers in bed, and exposes them to assembled gods.

l: hostage (from the nation of the Molossians), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A hostage from the Molossian nation is killed by Lycaon, cooked in boiling water and over fire, then served as body parts at a feast.

l: wolf (Lycaon's transformed form), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The wolf is Lycaon's transformed form after Jupiter's punishment. Garments become hair and arms become legs, yet vestiges of Lycaon remain: hoariness, violent features, bright eyes, and ferocity. It continues to desire slaughter and blood, attacking sheep.

l: savage Erinnys, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Savage Erinnys, a name for the Furies, reigns across earth, enforcing vengeance for human wickedness.

l: Lycaon's transformation into a wolf, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Lycaon's transformation occurs as Jupiter's punishment after Lycaon kills and serves the hostage. His garments become hair, his arms become legs, and he becomes a wolf while retaining vestiges of his former form.

l: vengeance, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Vengeance is carried out against Lycaon when Jupiter overturns his house and transforms him into a wolf. Jupiter also declares that all wicked men should soon feel the vengeance they deserve.

l: Pan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pan is a god or divinity, possibly associated with Egyptian worship of nature, yet possibly one of twelve Pans native to Greece and worshipped at Mendes. He loves and pursues Syrinx as she returns from the hill of Lycæus; when he seizes reeds rather than her, their sound charms him and he joins them with wax to form his first instrument, the Syrinx or Pandæan pipe, perhaps from reeds by the River Ladon. In poets’ embellished accounts he also falls in love with Echo, while another explanation presents Pan as a person seeking the cause of that phenomenon.

l: Epirus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Epirus lies by the Ambracian gulf, with the Molossi on its eastern side; situated very low, it was compared figuratively to the Infernal Regions and proposed as Aidoneus’s kingdom.

l: Tisiphone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Tisiphone, a Fury and daughter of Night, serves Juno’s vengeance. Leaving the infernal realms with gore-stained torch, blood-red cloak, snakes, and poison, she infects Athamas and Ino with madness, rage, and murderous intent.

l: wolf, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The wolf is presented as Lycaon’s transformed form, shunned by men and animals, a fugitive and wanderer compared with Cain’s punishment.

l: human sacrifice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Human sacrifice is central to the explanation of Lycaon’s story: Lycaon is said to have served human flesh to Jupiter, and the second Lycaon is said to have sacrificed human victims at Lycosura. The tradition is presented as a possible source of the story told by the poet.

l: frankincense, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Frankincense is a gum used as an offering: burned in sacrifice to Gods, its sweet smoke was thought to reach the heavens; Persia and Arabia are especially fertile in it.

l: rain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Rain is released from the whole tract of Heaven as Jupiter's chosen means of punishment. It falls in torrents after the South Wind squeezes the hanging clouds, beating down the standing corn and contributing to the universal flood.

l: Parnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Parnassus is a lofty, shady mountain with two peaks, rising beyond the clouds. During Deucalion’s deluge, its top alone remained uncovered as the sea covered other places. Deucalion, Pyrrha, and some subjects fled there, rested there, and remained until the waters abated.

l: Mount Ararat, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_the_site_of Noah's ark [where the ark rested] Mount Ararat is identified as the likely counterpart of Parnassus in the tradition followed by Ovid, because Noah’s ark was said to have rested there.

l: the flood of Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The flood of Deucalion, subject of Ovid’s narrative, covers the earth with sea and heavenly rain; Deucalion and Pyrrha survive. As its waters recede, they leave slime, from which reptiles arise before the sun dissipates noxious exhalations.

l: flood of Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Noah’s flood is compared with the flood of Deucalion. Both accounts include virtuous survivors, a solemn offering or altar after deliverance, and a promise or claim that the flood would be the last.

l: Triton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Triton, a minor sea god and son of Neptune and Amphitrite, is depicted with a human upper body and fish tail. Standing above the deep, he precedes and announces Neptune: at command, his shell’s sound makes the waters stop and retreat.

l: Phocis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phocis separates the Aonian and Actaean regions, once fruitful land containing Delphi and Mount Parnassus, then becomes sea and a wide plain of sudden waters during the deluge.

l: waters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_receding the Earth [after Neptune's command] The waters overflow the world and cover the Earth. At Neptune's command and after Triton's signal, they retreat: the rivers return to their channels, subside, and reveal the hills and woods.

l: the restoration of the world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: restores the world [after the deluge] The restoration of the world begins when Jupiter disperses the clouds and Neptune causes the waters to retreat. The rivers return to their channels, the hills and woods reappear, and the world is again visible, though desolate.

l: the conch shell, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Triton's shell, the buccina, is a hollow-wreathed trumpet widening from its lowest twist; at Neptune's command Triton sounds waters' retreat.

l: Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pluto is a god, son of Saturn, king of the shades, and ruler of the Infernal Regions. He may originally have been king of a separate kingdom; after being deified, he retains sovereignty. In the division of the universe he receives the last lot, the infernal regions, and rules a triple kingdom. Also called Dis as god of the Earth, he is confounded with Aidoneus because their realms are similar. Fearing that Typhœus's struggles could split the earth and expose the underworld, he cautiously surveys Sicily from a chariot drawn by black horses. Cupid wounds him in the breast with a barbed arrow. He sees Proserpina gathering flowers near Henna, falls in love, seizes her, and carries her away in his chariot. When Cyane reproaches him, he forces a way through her stream by throwing his sceptre into it and descends toward Tartarus. Proserpina becomes associated with his dominions and is identified as his husband in the Infernal Regions. Some accounts say he punishes Ascalaphus, while others connect the story to Erectheus's oracle and a required sacrifice of Proserpina.

l: Bœotia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bœotia is a country and region where Cadmus settles, named by Phœbus’s oracle when a heifer lies down. It contains Aonia and Anthedon. Its name is attributed either to βοῦς or Bœotus, and its territory is troubled by the dragon Cadmus slays.

l: Delphi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Delphi is a place near the Crissæan plain, containing Phœbus’s oracle and hosting Pythian games; Earth, then Themis, gave oracles there before Apollo’s worship, and Cadmus consults it.

l: Themis's response, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: An instruction from Themis directs Deucalion and Pyrrha to prepare and throw their great mother’s bones behind them, later understood as casting earth’s stones.

l: stones as ancestors of humanity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Stones, interpreted as the bones of earth and as children of Mount Parnassus survivors, are cast behind Deucalion and Pyrrha after the inundation. They gradually lose hardness, their earthy and humid parts becoming human bodies while solid parts become bones and veins remain veins. Deucalion’s stones become men; Pyrrha’s become women.

l: repopulation of the earth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Repopulation of the earth occurs as Deucalion and Pyrrha, obeying Themis, cast stones behind them; the Gods transform them into men and women.

l: Plutarch, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Plutarch is a writer and interpreter who authored How to read the Poets. He explains ritual head coverings and interprets the Muses’ encounter with Pyreneus as hostility to learning, while also describing Phaëton as a Molossian king and astronomy student and locating his tomb by the Po.

l: rainfall and the flooding of Thessaly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: overflows Thessaly [in the same year; caused by a great quantity of rain] In the same year that the course of the Peneus was stopped, an immense quantity of rain fell and overflowed all Thessaly. Deucalion and some of his subjects survived by fleeing to Mount Parnassus.

l: Cecrops, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cecrops, born in Egypt, settles in Greece, is counted among Greeks, and becomes Athens’s two-shaped king before Cranaüs and father of Herse and daughters linked to Minerva’s worship.

l: Nile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A river with seven streams and yearly inundations, Nile marks Io's wanderings' utmost boundary; reaching its bank, she falls and appeals Heaven.

l: laurel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Laurel, a tree, begins absent at the first Pythian games and becomes the form Daphne takes after praying for rescue. Apollo adopts it as his sacred tree, wears its lasting foliage, and links it to his lyre and quiver. It accompanies Roman triumphs, guards oak at Augustus’s gate-posts, and stands faithfully before his doors.

l: Egypt, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Egypt is a fertile place annually overflowed by the Nile, whose inundations chiefly give it extraordinary soil fertility. It uses ivory and wood combs toothed on one side. Io’s wandering ends there, where a linen-wearing throng worships her as Isis; Epaphus goes there to reign. It is also said to supply corn to Greece during famine, alongside agricultural worship and mysteries.

l: Amphictyon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: precedes Erecthonius [in the order of succession] Amphictyon disputed the right to the crown of Athens with Ericthonius after Cranaus’s death. One account says Amphictyon initially prevailed but was later succeeded by Ericthonius, while Apollodorus says that Ericthonius dethroned him.

l: robber near Parnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A robber near Parnassus infests the neighborhood and molests sacrificial travelers until Apollo or a priest of Apollo destroys him; he is proposed as Python's historical figure.

l: Pythian games institution, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Pythian games arose, by historical interpretation, from destruction of a robber near Parnassus; probably a religious ceremony or musical contest honoring the Pythian God, later adding gymnastic and equestrian competitions.

l: Cupid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cupid, Venus's winged son and a God, wields a bow and a quiver of arrows with opposed effects. He conquers gods and deities of the deep, wounds Pluto at his mother's direction, and later avenges Apollo's mockery by shooting Apollo with desire and Daphne with repulsion, assigning Daphne to Apollo.

l: Apollo and Daphne's pursuit, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Apollo, driven by Cupid’s golden arrow, pursues Daphne through the woods while Cupid’s leaden arrow makes her flee love. Their chase, likened to a greyhound pursuing a hare, highlights his eagerness and her anxiety until she reaches the waters of Peneus.

l: Daphne's transformation into a laurel, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Daphne’s transformation from nymph into laurel begins when she prays for aid and torpor seizes her limbs. Bark covers her breasts, her hair becomes leaves, her arms branches, and her feet take root, though her elegance remains. The story may have been inspired by nearby laurels or by her name’s meaning.

l: Love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: causes Apollo and Daphne's pursuit [Apollo's love drives the pursuit] Love is presented as the force that makes Apollo pursue Daphne and as the cause of his wound. Apollo says that love cannot be cured by herbs, even though he is the discoverer of healing and the properties of simples.

l: Cupid's arrows, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cupid's arrows are weapons that conquer all, including gods; directed by Erycina, he chooses a particularly sharp, unerring arrow to use against Pluto, while their effects can repel or excite desire.

l: Lycia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Lycia is a fertile province in Asia Minor on the Mediterranean Sea, marked by heat, the Chimæra, Latona’s insult, and a miraculous lake.

l: Tempe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Tempe is a Hæmonian grove and Thessalian valley, enclosed by wood amid craggy rocks; Peneus flows through it, where the river and water Nymphs retreat, and swan-formed Cycneus frequents it.

l: darkness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: covers earth [far and wide] Darkness is spread over the earth by Jupiter. It enables him to arrest Io's flight.

l: Jupiter's pursuit of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter pursues Io after seeing her return from Inachus's stream, following her through Lerna and Lircæan plains before using darkness to stop her.

l: Jupiter's ravishment of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter, after darkening the earth and stopping Io's flight, ravishes Io by forcing her modesty.

l: Phœnicians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phœnicians, anciently called Achivi even after establishing themselves in Greece, are associated with a proposed Chiva-for-serpent explanation of Cadmus and Hermione. They settled in Sicily and named a willow-surrounded fountain Alphaga, “the fountain of the willows,” or Arith, “a stream.”

l: Isis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Isis is a chief Egyptian divinity and the restored, worshipped identity of Io after Juno permits her human form to return. Worshipped by linen-wearing Egyptians, her cult spread to foreign countries, including Greece, where she was identified with Io and, according to Banier, confused with Ceres and established at Eleusis by Triptolemus.

l: Crete, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Crete is an isle, also called Gortynian, identified as the island to which Jupiter carries Europa. Teutamus and some Pelasgians settle there, and it becomes the kingdom of Jupiter Asterius. Minos reigns, expands power through neighboring islands and surrounding seas, and prepares war against Athens after Androgeus dies; later, Procris flees to the second Minos’s court.

l: Osiris, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Osiris, also called Apis in the account of Io’s marriage, was born in Egypt and identified by Herodotus and Plutarch as the true, most ancient Bacchus. After death he was known as Serapis and numbered among Egypt’s deities; his worship passed to Greece and changed through Bacchic mysteries.

l: Argos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_under_the_tutelage_of Juno [according to Homer] Argos is identified as the kingdom of which Inachus was the first king. Io is described as Inachus's daughter.

l: the original story, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Io's story probably originated in Egypt but was altered by poetic tradition; Greek authors linked it to Isis worship, Jupiter's abduction, Epaphus's birth, Juno's jealousy, Argus, and cow-form passage.

l: transformation of Io into a cow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The transformation of Io into a sleek, snow-white cow begins when Jupiter changes Inachus’s daughter to hide her from Juno. Unable to speak or use her arms, Io communicates by lowing and writing with her foot. Greek writers link her cow-shaped passage to a ship’s cow figure and the name Bosphorus.

l: cow (Io), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Io is a snow-white cow praised by Juno, feeding and resting outdoors, drinking muddy streams, then tied by the neck and shut up at night.

l: Juno's discovery of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a discovery Juno notices that clouds have made the appearance of night during the day and realizes that they are not ordinary vapors. She searches for Jupiter, descends from heaven, and discovers Io in the form of a cow.

l: Juno's taking possession of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a taking possession [as a gift from Jupiter] Juno asks Jupiter for the cow as a gift, and he gives Io to her because refusing such a small gift would arouse suspicion. Juno then places Io in Argus's custody because she remains afraid that Jupiter may reclaim or steal her.

l: Argus's guard of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a guard [watchful] Argus keeps Io under constant surveillance with his hundred eyes, watching her even when he turns away. He lets her feed during the day, shuts her up at night, and ties a cord around her neck.

l: Mercury's mission to kill Argus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a mission [ordered by Jupiter] Jupiter sends Mercury to put Argus to death because Io's suffering can no longer be endured. Mercury approaches Argus disguised as a shepherd and tries to overpower his watchful eyes with the sound of his pipes and extended conversation.

l: Metamorphosis of Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a mythological story [a story whose explanation has been discussed previously] The Metamorphosis of Io is presented as a story whose details may reflect a true history altered by tradition and further disfigured by poetic imagination. The text says that tracing its original facts is extremely difficult.

l: myths, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_based_on history [frequently, with the history corrupted by tradition over time] Myths are described as mythological stories or fables that are frequently based on true history. According to the text, tradition, the passage of time, and the poets’ love of the marvellous can greatly alter their original form.

l: the Naiads, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Naiads, Syrinx’s watery sisters, answer her plea when Ladon stops her flight by changing her into reeds; they are possibly associated with an altar.

l: the river Ladon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arcadia's gentle, sandy Ladon stops Syrinx fleeing Pan, passes vast reed-filled banks, and flows placidly into Alpheus.

l: instrument (Pan's), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pan's instrument has seven unequal reeds, joined with wax, named after Syrinx; Pan makes it after wind murmurs sweetly among reeds, possibly from Ladon's banks.

l: the reeds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The reeds Pan seizes, believing he caught Syrinx, murmur in wind and become panpipes when unequal reeds are joined with wax.

l: Syrinx's flight, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Syrinx's flight through pathless places escapes Pan's pursuit until the river Ladon's waters stop her course.

l: Pan's pursuit of Syrinx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pan pursues Syrinx after falling in love with her. He follows her from the hill of Lycæus until she reaches the river Ladon, where he thinks he has caught her but grasps reeds instead.

l: Syrinx's transformation into reeds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by the Naiads When Syrinx is stopped by the river Ladon, she asks the Naiads to change her. They transform her into reeds, which Pan later uses to make his instrument.

l: the invention of the panpipes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pan makes the panpipes after Syrinx has been transformed into reeds. Hearing the wind's sound among them, he joins unequal reeds with wax, creating an instrument that bears Syrinx's name.

l: Egyptian fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Egyptian fable, apparently Egyptian in origin, was possibly imported into the works of Grecian poets.

l: Syrinx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_styled_daughter_of Ladon [possibly because the instrument was formed from his banks' produce] Syrinx was the name of the Syrinx, or Pandæan pipe, which Pan probably invented. She may have been called the daughter of the River Ladon because Pan perhaps formed the instrument from reeds growing on its banks.

l: peacock (Juno's bird), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Juno’s bird receives Argus’s eyes as starry gems on its feathers, filling its tail; its eye-like spots are said to resemble human eyes.

l: Clymene, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Clymene is a sea Nymph, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, queen of the Ethiopians, and mother of Phaëton and his sisters. After hearing Phaëton’s account of reproaches, she swears that the Sun begot him and directs him to the Sun’s dwelling. After Phaëton dies, she searches for his limbs, finds his bones abroad, mourns at his tomb, and tries to save her daughters as they become trees.

l: Phaëton's sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phaëton's sisters, daughters of the Sun, mourn Phaëton day and night near his tomb, calling his name and beating their breasts. Overcome by grief at his fate, they end their lives as their bodies gradually transform into poplars; some writers say they become larch trees instead.

l: Io's restoration to human form, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: After Juno is pacified, Io regains human shape as her cowlike features return to human form; only her whiteness remains as she rises on two feet.

l: Io's worship as Isis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Io, restored and named Isis, is worshipped in Egypt as a goddess by linen-wearing Egyptians.

l: Io's wandering, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Io’s wandering, driven by Juno’s Fury and invisible stings through the whole earth, ends at the Nile in Egypt.

l: Phaëton's journey to the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phaëton's journey begins after Clymene confirms the Sun is his father; he travels toward the Sun's dwelling, passing his own Æthiopians and the Indians beneath the Sun's rays.

l: Ethiopia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Æthiopia, regarded as a region of the East, contains Cepheus’s land and is proposed as the setting where Perseus finds Andromeda exposed and Cepheus and Cassiope rule, though Africa’s coast is considered more probable.

l: Hierax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_transformed_into spar-hawk [according to some mythologists] Hierax awoke Argus after Mercury had lulled him to sleep. Mercury then transformed Hierax into a spar-hawk.

l: Mercury's killing of Argus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Mercury kills Argus with a stone after Hierax wakes Argus from sleep Mercury had induced.

l: Hierax's transformation into a spar-hawk, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Hierax's transformation is an event in which, after Hierax awoke Argus, Mercury turned Hierax into a spar-hawk.

l: Sun's palace, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun’s palace stands on radiant columns, richly decorated with gold, carbuncle, ivory, silver, and Mulciber’s carvings of sea, Earth, Heaven, deities, cities, animals, and Zodiac signs.

l: the Sun's chariot, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun’s chariot is a magnificent solar vehicle made by Vulcan, with gold on its axle-tree, poles, and wheel circumference, silver spokes, and chrysolites and gems on its yoke. Suited to the Sun horses and carrying light, it is driven by Phaëton in the fable. Too lightly burdened, it becomes unstable, leaps and rises through the air, and its course burns mountains, rivers, and lands. Jupiter’s lightning destroys it, scattering its reins, axle-tree, broken wheels, spokes, and fragments.

l: the horses (Phaëton's chariot), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun horses are a fiery, winged team of four, Pyroeis, Eoüs, Æthon, and Phlegon, drawing Apollo’s chariot and fed on ambrosia. Hard to restrain, they sense unusual lightness, abandon their regular track, and run in fury. After Phaëton’s death, terrified and maddened, they are subdued and reproached by Phœbus.

l: Bear, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a Constellation The Great Bear is identified with the constellation formed when Jupiter places Calisto among the stars. The explanation says that its never setting may have inspired Juno’s request that it not be received into the Ocean.

l: Ætna, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ætna, a mountain, presses on Typhœus’s head to imprison him beneath earth; rich in sulphur and bituminous matter, it often emits flames and is linked to violent earth shocks.

l: Mount Cithæron, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Mount Cithæron, a mountain of Bœotia famed for Bacchic orgies, hosts rites filled with singing and worshippers’ cries. Pentheus goes there to interrupt and chastise the Bacchantes’ festival, but is dismembered in its woods.

l: river Po, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The river Po is identified by Plutarch as the location of Phaëton’s tomb. Lucian later inquired there about the swans and amber-producing poplars described in the tradition.

l: Phaëton's failed chariot ride, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phaëton’s one-day attempt to drive the solar chariot becomes an allegory of a rash young man’s wilful folly. Unable to control the horses or recognize the route, he drops the reins at the threatening Scorpion. The chariot wanders through unknown sky, rising and plunging near earth, and its uncontrolled course causes the world’s destruction.

l: world's destruction, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Universal burning and drought scorch nations, cities, forests, mountains, rivers, and seas; rivers, Nile, and Ocean dry, exposing Tartarus through Earth's cracks, until Earth's plea seeks rescue from threatened universal chaos.

l: Corinth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Corinth, also called Ephyre and Bimaris, borders the Aegean and Ionian Seas and contains the king’s palace. Ruled by Creon, it receives Medea for her conflict with Jason, Glauce, and Creon; she burns the palace, consuming the bride and Creon. In one account, Corinthians kill her children, and the Gods send plague.

l: Phaëton's fall, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phaëton is hurled headlong and carried in a long tract through the air, like a star that appears to fall from a clear sky. Eridanus receives him in a distant part of the world. Phaëton’s fate caused his mother and sisters great grief. Their grief was said to have led to their deaths and transformation.

l: Phaëton's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phaëton dies when Jupiter's lightning strikes him and his chariot, prompted by the Sun's grievance. His smoking body is entombed by the Hesperian Naiads; Cycnus mourns beside the Eridanus, while his father abandons labor and blames the steeds.

l: Eridanus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Eridanus receives Phaëton's body after his fall, far from his country, and bathes his foaming face.

l: the Hesperian Naiads, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Hesperian Naiads, Italy’s Naiads Phaëthusa, Lampetie, and Phœbe, gather at Phaëton’s smoking tomb.

l: tomb of Phaëton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The tomb of Phaëton stands on the banks of the river Po, containing his buried body and marked by marble bearing his name. The Hesperian Naiads place him there after his failed chariot attempt; Clymene mourns, and the tomb is linked to his mother’s and sisters’ grief and deaths.

l: the sisters' transformation into trees, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: produces the poplars The sisters' feet become stiff, roots hold them, leaves replace their hair, and their limbs become branches. Bark gradually covers their bodies until only their mouths remain uncovered, and the transformation ends as bark covers their final words.

l: the poplars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The poplars are transformed sisters of Phaëton on the banks of the river Po; their newly formed branches produce tears that harden in the sun into amber they distill.

l: the sisters' tears, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: become amber [hardening in the sun] The sisters' tears continue to flow from their new branches after their transformation. The tears harden in the sun and become amber.

l: amber, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Amber, hardened tears from sisters’ branches and poplars, is received by Eridanus and sent to be worn by Latian matrons.

l: the sun having stood still upon Gibeon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The sun having stood still upon Gibeon is a possible faint reference to a tradition where Joshua commands the sun to stand still during divine vengeance upon the Amorites.

l: the shadow returning ten degrees backward, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The shadow returns ten degrees backward, measured by the sun-dial of Ahaz and presented as a possible faint reference to that movement.

l: Cycnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cycnus is a king of Liguria, son of Sthenelus, ruler of the Ligurians and their cities, and a friend and maternal-side relative of Phaëton. After leaving his kingdom to mourn Phaëton beside the Eridanus and the wood augmented by the sisters, he may die of grief and is changed into a swan. As a swan, he avoids the heavens and air, abhors fire, and frequents pools, lakes, and streams.

l: Cycnus's transformation into a swan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a transformation [into a swan] Cycnus’s transformation changes his voice, hair, neck, feet, sides, and mouth: feathers appear, his neck lengthens, a membrane joins his reddening toes, and his mouth becomes a bill without a point. The transformation makes him a bird that avoids the heavens, air, and fire and instead frequents pools, lakes, and streams.

l: swan, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Swan is a bird and Cycnus’s new form, taken through grief and attachment to Phaëton. Avoiding the heavens and air after fire from there, it chooses streams, pools, and wide lakes; none were reported on the Po.

l: the fire, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_abhorrent_to Cycnus [after his transformation] The fire is associated with the heavens and is remembered by Cycnus as having been unjustly sent from there. Cycnus, in his new bird form, abhors fire and chooses streams as its opposite.

l: Phaëton and his sisters tradition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The tradition says that Phaëton’s sisters died from grief near his tomb and were changed into trees that distilled amber. Lucian said that the inhabitants near the river Po did not know this tradition.

l: the Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Nymphs notice Calisto’s injured honor, perceive her fault, and witness Diana expose her pregnancy while bathing.

l: the violation of Calisto's vow of chastity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Jupiter's seduction and assault of Calisto Calisto’s vow of chastity is violated when Jupiter, disguised as Diana, embraces and assaults her. The violation becomes evident through her shame, altered behavior, and eventual pregnancy.

l: Jupiter's seduction and assault of Calisto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: occurs_while Jupiter assumes the form of Diana [as a deception] Jupiter’s deception begins when he assumes Diana’s appearance and approaches Calisto as one of Diana’s companions. He kisses and embraces her, prevents her from resisting, and assaults her before leaving the grove.

l: Little Bear, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a Constellation The Little Bear is identified with the constellation formed when Jupiter places Arcas among the stars. The explanation suggests that Arcas’s early death may have been the origin of this constellation.

l: raven, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The raven, once a white bird praised for beautiful feathers, reports Coronis's infidelity to Apollo. Apollo blames and punishes it for its garrulous report, forbidding it among the white birds. It changes from white to black, becoming a bird with black wings.

l: Cicero, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: tells_of Mercury [several persons in ancient times named Mercury] Cicero is said to have reported that several persons in ancient times were named Mercury.

l: transformation of Calisto into a bear, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a punishment [inflicted by Juno] Juno seizes Calisto by the hair and throws her to the ground, where her arms grow black hair, her hands become hooked claws, and her mouth becomes that of a bear. Calisto retains her human understanding but loses the power of speech.

l: placement of Calisto and Arcas among the stars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: occurs_in the heavens When Arcas is about to kill Calisto without recognizing her, Jupiter prevents the act and carries both of them into the heavens. He makes them neighboring constellations.

l: the raven's transformation from white to black, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A Fable in which a raven’s white plumage turns black as punishment for garrulity: its prattling and disclosure of hidden matters, attributed to its tongue, cause the change, though history offers no foundation for the story.

l: Coronis's infidelity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_infidelity_of Coronis [with the youth of Hæmonia] Coronis’s infidelity consists of lying down with a youth of Hæmonia. The raven tells Apollo about it, leading Apollo to kill Coronis.

l: virgin (Apollo's favorite; later changed into a crow), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A royal virgin, daughter of Coroneus and Apollo’s favorite, watches three virgins guarding Ericthonius. She reports Aglauros’s discovery of the basket’s secret to Minerva; her fidelity brings ruin, and she is changed into a crow, then assigned as Minerva’s faultless companion.

l: Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ericthonius is a fabled offspring born without a mother, variously described as son or foster-child of Athene, son of Cranaë, or connected with Vulcan and Earth. Minerva aids his birth, encloses him in a basket, and gives him to three virgins; another account says he was exposed and found in a temple of Minerva and Vulcan. With deformed legs, he is said to have invented chariots and to be half serpent. After disputing the crown with Amphictyon, he dethrones and succeeds him as Athens’ fourth king, institutes the Panathenæa, and after death is received into heaven as Auriga.

l: the three virgins entrusted with Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cecrops’ daughters entrusted by Minerva with Ericthonius’ basket; Pandrosos and Herse remain faithful, but Aglauros opens it against injunction.

l: Pandrosos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pandrosos, third daughter of Cecrops, faithfully obeys Minerva, observes the basket containing Ericthonius without treachery, and after death receives a temple near Minerva's temple.

l: God of the Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: God of the Ocean sees a virgin, desires her, entreats her unsuccessfully, then prepares violence and pursues her as she flees along the seashore.

l: Nyctimene, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Nyctimene, child of Nycteus, commits incest with her father and is changed into a bird of the night for the crime. Ashamed, she avoids human gaze and light, conceals herself in darkness, and is expelled from the sky by other birds. She succeeds the crow in a former honor.

l: basket containing Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: contains dragon beside Ericthonius [the dragon is beside the child] Minerva makes the basket from Actæan twigs and gives it to Pandrosos, Herse, and Aglauros. She orders them not to inquire into its secret, but Aglauros unties its knots and looks inside.

l: dragon beside Ericthonius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: When Aglauros opens the basket, the three virgins see a child and a dragon extended beside him.

l: crow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The virgin is changed into a crow and is placed after the bird of the night. She says that her punishment may warn birds not to incur dangers through their chattering.

l: the basket's secret, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Minerva forbids the three virgins to investigate the basket's secret. Its contents are revealed when Aglauros opens it: a child and a dragon beside him.

l: fidelity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The virgin says that her fidelity was her ruin because she reported Aglauros's discovery to Minerva. She presents the report as an act of loyalty rather than treachery.

l: the crow's punishment and banishment, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: For telling Minerva what Aglauros had done, the virgin is said to have been banished from Minerva's protection and placed after the bird of the night. Her punishment is connected with her chattering about what she had seen.

l: the attempted assault by the God of the Ocean, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_attempted_by God of the Ocean [against the virgin] The God of the Ocean pursues the virgin along the shore after she rejects his soft words and attempts to use violence. She flees across the yielding sand and invokes gods and men, but no mortal hears her.

l: the virgin's transformation into a crow, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A fable of a virgin, Apollo's favorite, transformed into a crow after divine assistance. As she raises her arms, black feathers cover her and her body changes; she runs, flies, and becomes Minerva's faultless companion. Notes describe the change as punishment for an overly faithful report and offer no historical foundation.

l: Panathenæa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Panathenæa was a festival instituted at Athens by Ericthonius, celebrated there with games won by Androgeus, and in time adopted by the whole of Greece.

l: incest, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The incest concerns Nyctimene’s criminal passion for and defilement of the bed of her father. The Gods punish it by transforming Nyctimene into an owl.

l: Nyctimene's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a transformation into an owl [inflicted as punishment] The Gods transform Nyctimene into an owl as punishment for her incest. Afterward, she avoids light and human gaze and is expelled from the sky by the other birds.

l: Coronis's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Coronis’s death occurs when Apollo’s arrow pierces her breast; she removes it, bleeds, speaks final words, and dies in coldness.

l: Coronis's funeral, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_prepared_for Coronis [with a funeral pile and due obsequies] A funeral pile is prepared for Coronis, and her limbs are about to be burned. Apollo pours perfumes on her breast, embraces her, performs the due obsequies, and removes the child from the flames.

l: the raven's report, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: reports Coronis's infidelity [to Apollo] The raven’s report tells Apollo that he has seen Coronis lying down with a youth of Hæmonia. Apollo listens to the report, kills Coronis, and later blames the raven for causing his sorrow.

l: Fables, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Fables about Coronis and the raven may describe two people unknown to history, perhaps from as early as the daughters of Cecrops; they are presented as seemingly related to that earlier time.

l: daughters of Cecrops, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The daughters of Cecrops hesitated to encourage Minerva’s worship, probably when it was introduced into Attica; portrayed as punished for impiety, they went mad and threw themselves from a tower.

l: Fates, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Fates, three Goddesses, possess prophecy, stop Ocyrrhoe from revealing more of the future, and will cut Chiron’s life threads.

l: Ocyrrhoe's transformation into a mare, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ocyrrhoe’s divine transformation into the mare Enippe is a wondrous change, possibly explaining her exceptional riding and horse-handling skill. Desiring grass and open plains, her human form withdraws: fingers become a hoof, face and neck lengthen, hair becomes tail and mane, and her voice and shape change.

l: prophecy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The prophecy concerns Æsculapius’s healing power, his restoration of the dead, his punishment by his grandsire’s bolts, and his return from death to godhood. It also concerns Chiron’s eventual mortality and Ocyrrhoe’s own transformation, which begins before she can complete her speech.

l: Apollo's cattle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Apollo's cattle stray into Pylos, are stolen and hidden by Mercury, then located by Battus.

l: the theft of Apollo's cattle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Mercury steals Apollo's cattle while Apollo is away; Battus first conceals the theft for a cow, then exposes it for greater reward.

l: Touchstone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Touchstone is a hard stone bearing undeserved old disgrace, formed when Mercury turns Battus into stone after Battus betrays him.

l: Battus's transformation into a touchstone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Battus betrays Mercury's theft for an additional reward, so Mercury turns his perjured breast to stone, creating the Touchstone marked by an old disgrace.

l: Centaurs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Centaurs are fabulous half-human, half-horse monsters, perhaps originating as Thessaly’s first horsemen before horseback riding shaped their monstrous reputation.

l: Argonauts' voyage for the recovery of the Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Argonauts' voyage is a remarkable voyage that departs from Iolcos, stops at Lemnos, later reaches Bithynia, rescues Phineus from the Harpies, and arrives at Colchis. There Jason performs Æetes' dangerous labors with Medea's help, puts the dragon to sleep, takes the Golden Fleece, and returns triumphantly to Iolcos.

l: Envy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Envy is a personification of envy who lives in a concealed, sunless, cold, dark cave. She eats vipers, carries a thorn-wreathed staff and black poison, and suffers at others’ success. Commanded by Minerva, she poisons Aglauros by showing her Herse, Herse’s marriage, and Mercury, causing jealousy.

l: Mercury's pursuit of Herse, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a pursuit [conducted through Aglauros] Mercury pursues Herse after seeing her return from the sacred ceremony, circling above the Actaean towers before approaching her house. He asks Aglauros to support his pursuit and to help him gain access to Herse.

l: Aglauros's demand for payment, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a demand [for assistance in Mercury's suit] Aglauros refuses to assist Mercury unless he gives her gold of great weight. She makes this demand while asking about his identity and the reason for his visit, and then forces him to go out of the house.

l: Diana, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Diana, daughter of Eubalus, was born on Delos and also called Ortygia. Particularly fond of the chase, she was associated with plague among women. She was said to kill Niobe's daughters, while Melibœa and Amycle survived after appeasing her or recovering from plague.

l: jealousy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jealousy, a secret grief imposed on Aglauros by Envy, targets fortunate Herse and Mercury’s probable love, tormenting Aglauros day and night until she wastes away.

l: tradition, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_based_on facts [of so ordinary a nature] The tradition concerning Mercury, Herse, and Aglauros was probably built on facts of an ordinary nature.

l: Envy's poison, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A noxious venom breathed into Aglauros, spreading through bones and lungs, causing grief, wasting, stiffness, and stopped speech and breath.

l: Herse's marriage, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A fortunate marriage involving Mercury’s beautiful appearance unfolds as Envy repeatedly provokes Aglauros’s jealousy.

l: Aglauros's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Aglauros’s transformation is a deadly change into a bloodless stone statue, beginning with heaviness, numbness, stiffening knees, and pallid veins, then spreading until her whole form becomes stone.

l: temple of Pandrosos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_near Minerva (Tritonia/Pallas) [near Minerva’s temple] The temple of Pandrosos was built after her death near the temple of Minerva, in honor of her continued faithfulness to the Goddess.

l: worship of Pallas/Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_introduced_into Attica The introduction of the worship of Pallas or Minerva into Attica may have caused the daughters of Cecrops to hesitate to support the innovation. The explanation suggests that the story of their punishment was promulgated to condemn their impiety.

l: Jupiter's transformation into a bull, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a transformation Jupiter lays aside his divine authority and assumes the appearance of a beautiful white bull. The bull has a muscular neck, small transparent horns, and a peaceful, nonthreatening expression.

l: Jupiter's abduction of Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter's abduction of Europa is an abduction, explained as Jupiter Asterius's forced voyage carrying Europa away. It begins when Europa unknowingly sits on a bull's back; he enters the water, carries her from shore across the ocean toward Crete, and may reflect a bull-figurehead ship or related names and words.

l: Danaë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Danaë, daughter of Acrisius and mother of Perseus, is confined by Acrisius to avert a prophecy, yet conceives Perseus in a shower of gold, attributed to Jupiter or, in another account, to Prœtus through bribed guards.

l: Jupiter Asterius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter Asterius, son of Teutamus, is associated with Europa's abduction and ruled Crete as its first king amid Pelasgian settlement, said to have reigned about B.C. 1400.

l: Hellotia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Hellotia is a festival honoring Europa, instituted after her death and named from the name she received after death.

l: festival honoring Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_instituted_for Europa [after her death] A festival was instituted to honor Europa after her death. Hesychius calls this festival Hellotia.

l: the oracle of Delphi, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: An oracle given by Phœbus issues commands: it directs the building of Thebes, sends Archias with Corinthians to Syracuse, and guides Cadmus to found Bœotia by following an unyoked heifer.

l: heifer, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The heifer, a cow never yoked or marked for servitude, has no keeper and is free from the crooked plough; she leads Cadmus across fields and the Cephisus, then lies down.

l: dragon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The dragon is a golden, crested creature sacred to Mars, hidden in a cavern in an ancient grove and guarding Mars's fountain. It has fiery eyes, a poison-swollen body, three tongues, and teeth in three rows; notes describe it as enormous and able to kill by sting, coils, or poisonous breath. When Cadmus's companions disturb the grove, it emerges, attacks them, and battles Cadmus. After leaving Sidon, Cadmus pierces its throat with a spear, driving it into an oak and killing it. Cadmus then sows its teeth as an unknown seed and later questions whether it was sacred. Accounts alternatively call it a serpent, or a king named Draco and a son of Mars.

l: the grove, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Unprofaned grove with Mars’s fountain is entered by Tyrian men; after disturbing its water, Cadmus finds them dead beneath a victorious dragon.

l: Telephassa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Telephassa, wife of Agenor and mother of Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa, accompanied Cadmus in Thrace before dying before Delphi.

l: Thrace, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Formerly called Scython, Thrace contains Ciconians' walls; Boreas carries Orithyïa there after abduction, despite Tereus and Thracians' opposition.

l: Europe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Europe is a place whose name is variously attributed to Europa or to the fair complexion of its inhabitants.

l: genealogy of Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: According to Apollodorus, Libya had two sons by Neptune, Belus and Agenor; Agenor married Telephassa, and their children were Cadmus, Phœnix, Cilix, and Europa. Other writers made Europa the daughter of Phœnix and the granddaughter of Agenor.

l: Cadmus's companions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cadmus's companions are Tyrian men who go to the fountain of Mars for water, where its guarding dragon attacks, devours, and kills them.

l: fountain of Mars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A fountain associated with Mars, where Cadmus's companions draw water until a guarding dragon emerges from a deep cave.

l: the dragon's teeth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The dragon’s teeth are sown by Cadmus in furrows under turned-up earth at Minerva’s direction. They produce earth-born armed men, emerging with spears, helmets, shields, and other weapons. In one interpretation they are the dragon’s subjects; another treats them as symbols of soldiers or brass-pointed javelins.
